passes.do: Wrap the annotated layers - retry, timeout, logging, tracing, metrics, cache - outside the node so its graph is unchanged. Attach the scope so every acquired resource is released on every path including error and cancellation. Then behaviors of kind `effect`, config and migration wiring, docs stating invariants, scaffolding removed, full suite run.
passes.exit: Full suite green. Repo shippable. Removing any layer would not require editing the happy path. Every acquired resource has a structural release. The node's purpose still describes every behavior it now has - if not, record the widening or the split.

exit_criteria: All four passes complete for this node, in order.
phases.loop_back_if: The code contradicts the traced contract. Return to `trace` or `triage` rather than patching around it.

phases.title: Re-trace the changed node
phases.purpose: The graph is different now. Walk X and Z again from what you just edited.
ask: Who calls this node now? Anyone new, or anyone the first trace missed?
What does it call now? Any dependency added during implementation?
Did the actual contract land where the triage predicted, or did it drift during implementation?

Does the code match the annotated graph - same A order, same E enumeration, same R? If it does not, the implementation is wrong, not the graph. Correct the code, or correct the annotation deliberately and say why.

At flow level: does the actual cross-node call order match the flow's node_sequence? A per-node conformance check passes happily while the flow through them is wrong, so this is the check that catches a reordered or short-circuited path.
Do the callers marked no_change still pass, untouched?
exit_criteria: Actual contract recorded and compared against the predicted contract_delta.

Conformance checked: the code's call graph, error enumeration and dependency list match the `channels` annotation. Any divergence is resolved in one direction or the other, never left as a silent mismatch.
Any node newly discovered is triaged and appended to the ordered change set.
Every no_change caller still passes.
phases.loop_back_if: A no_change node broke, or an untraced caller appeared. Return to `trace`. Do not edit the failing test to agree with the new code.

phases.title: Close the loop
phases.purpose: Run the checks and let them decide. Closure is observed, not asserted.

runner.why: Cheapest and most localizing first. A red unit test names the node; a red acceptance check only says the requirement is unmet.
runner.commands: Taken from the check manifest recorded at `acceptance`, run verbatim. The agent does not improvise the command, so the same thing is run every turn.
runner.on_all_green: The requirement is closed. Not because it looks done - because the check that was red before any code was written is now green.
runner.on_acceptance_red_with_units_green: The behaviors are right and the requirement is still unmet. This is the most informative failure in the method: either the graph delta missed a node, or the requirement was misunderstood at `language`. Read the expected-versus-observed diff before touching code.
runner.on_flaky: A check that passes on retry is not green. Fix the determinism - pinned time, seeded data, stable selectors, no sleeps - or the loop's closure means nothing.

ask: Did the acceptance check flip from red to green, and is that recorded with the command and output?
Are all behavior tests green, and every no_change invariant still passing?

For each ambiguity: did its assertion pass? An assumed expectation whose assertion passed is now confirmed; one that failed means the assumption was wrong, which is a requirement finding rather than a bug.
Which `assumed` bases had no assertion at all, and should the user see them now?
Did this turn produce new information - a different failure, a new node, a new behavior, a falsified assumption, a resolved unsure? If not, halt and escalate rather than spending another turn.
exit_criteria: The acceptance check went red to green, with the command and output recorded. A requirement marked done without that transition is not done - it is claimed.
Every behavior test green, every no_change invariant still passing, no check passing only on retry.
Every ambiguity resolved as confirmed, falsified, or escalated - falsified assumptions reported to the user rather than quietly corrected.
Requirement marked done, or blocked with the reason, or halted and escalated because a turn produced no new information.
Visualization regenerated.
phases.next: Next requirement by dependency order -> `acceptance` for it, reusing the glossary from `language`. If none remain, ascend to the task tier.

phases.title: Drift check
phases.purpose: Confirm the trace still describes the code, after someone else changed it.
phases.trigger: On resume of any trace file. After any fetch, pull, merge or rebase. Before the first edit of each session. Before ascending a tier.
ask: Run `design.py rebuild` first: the folds must match the log before any drift question is meaningful.
Which traced paths changed between traced_at_commit and now?
For each: does the recorded contract hash still match?
Did any traced node get renamed, moved or deleted?
Does each no_change invariant still hold in the new code?
For every seam: has the far side shipped since I traced it? Git in this repo cannot answer that - check the schema artifact's version, the provider's release or image tag, or run the contract test.

seam_drift.why_it_is_different: A seam can drift with no commit in this repo at all. The provider deployed; nothing here changed. This is the failure mode a git-only drift check silently misses.
how: Pin what you can: commit the OpenAPI or proto artifact, and diff it on fetch.
Run the contract test - a red contract test is drift, not a flaky test.
Compare the provider's deployed version against the version recorded on the seam at trace time.
For a database seam, re-read the schema: a column, index or constraint added by someone else's migration is drift.
seam_drift.outcome: Treat provider-side drift on a seam you consume exactly like `contract_drifted` on a local node: re-triage this seam and everything downstream of it.

method: git diff --name-only <traced_at_commit>...HEAD, intersected with the node paths. Three-dot, so a divergent branch compares against the merge base.
For each hit: compare blob_sha first (cheap). If changed, re-read the symbol and recompute the contract hash.
For a missing path: git log --follow --diff-filter=RD -- <path> to find the rename or deletion.

outcomes.contract_intact: The file changed but the contract did not. Update blob_sha and traced_at_commit. Proceed.
outcomes.contract_drifted: Re-triage this node and re-expand from it, since the delta may now propagate differently.
outcomes.node_moved: Update the path, keep the verdict and history, note the rename.
outcomes.node_gone: Return to `locate`. The seed assumption may no longer hold.
outcomes.invariant_broken: A no_change node's invariant no longer holds in the new code. Treat as a conflict to resolve with the other author, not as a test to fix.

exit_criteria: Every stale node has an outcome recorded. traced_at_commit updated for the whole trace.

two_drifts.trace_vs_commit: A trace file describes the code at traced_at_commit. Someone else's merge invalidates it. This is the git-diff check below.
two_drifts.snapshot_vs_codebase: A model snapshot describes the domain as understood then. It is never updated - it is a record, and a record does not drift. What can be wrong is applying an old snapshot to today's code, so a new task captures its own.

phases.title: Ascend a tier
phases.purpose: Close the task, update the task graph, choose the next.
ask: Which keywords led to the change set, and which were dead ends?
Where did the trace get it wrong, and which stop condition failed?
Which glossary terms were added or corrected, and does the code now agree with them?
Which dead alias is now worth retiring, and is that a follow-up task?
Which tasks are now unblocked, and which is next by dependency?
Does index.md report a divergence introduced by this task - one term defined two ways? That is a finding to resolve or escalate, not a merge to perform.
exit_criteria: The ticket is marked closed through `design.py close`; the log and every snapshot stay in place.
index.md is regenerated and any divergence it reports is either resolved or escalated with a reason.
Task tier statuses and the rendered graph are current.
Next task selected by dependency, or the ticket is done.

greenfield_variant.when: keywords hit nothing because the capability does not exist
greenfield_variant.how: Trace the closest analogue feature. Its subgraph is the template: same roles, same layering, same test shape. The change set mixes new nodes at the analogue's positions with existing nodes that must accept them.
greenfield_variant.note: The entrypoint, wiring and config nodes always already exist, and they are where new features break old ones.

vocabulary.problem: The rule is to mine the model from existing code, and greenfield has none to mine. This is the one place in the method where naming is invention rather than discovery, so it gets guardrails instead of a prohibition.
sources_in_order: The domain expert's or PM's own words for the concept - transcribe them before paraphrasing.
Sibling contexts' glossaries in this repo: a term already ratified elsewhere beats a new one.
The analogue feature's vocabulary, adapted - if refunds exist and you are adding credits, follow the refund vocabulary's shape.
Industry or regulatory language, when the domain has a standard word - the domain did not start with this codebase.
Last resort: coin it, and mark it as coined.

ratification.rule: An invented term is provisional until ratified. It is recorded with provenance `invented`, a proposer, and a ratified_by that starts null.
ratification.must_appear_in: the acceptance check's name and the behavior statements, so the new word shows up in a committed artifact where a human will read it rather than only in a state file
ratification.gate: The requirement gate reports every unratified invented term alongside the acceptance check. It does not block - it surfaces. A term nobody has agreed to is a rename waiting, and renames are cheapest before the code exists.
ratification.review_flag: unratified terms are listed at `close` as the first item, since the glossary is the artifact that outlives the ticket

vocabulary.still_trace: Greenfield does not skip the trace. The entrypoint, router, wiring, config, migrations and CI nodes all exist already, and the new capability must attach to them - that attachment is where new features break old ones.

state.shape: One flat directory. Everything in it is temporal, captured at a commit, and never edited by a later task.
state.source_of_truth: <ref>.log.jsonl - an append-only decision log. One line per decision. A reversal is a new line that supersedes an earlier one, never an edit to it.

derived.<ref>.<task-slug>.model.json: the domain as understood for that task
derived.<ref>.<task-slug>.graph.md: the rendered view of that task
derived.index.md: recall across every model snapshot, with divergences flagged

state.rule: Never hand-edit a derived file. The next append rebuilds it and the edit is lost. Decide through the CLI; read the folds.
state.recall: There is no shared mutable model, so there is nothing to forget to update and nothing to go stale. Two tasks that define one term differently produce a divergence in index.md - a finding, not a write that silently wins.

tooling.why: Hand-written JSON is how state ends up malformed and phases end up half-recorded. Every subcommand validates, appends one decision, re-folds and renders - so the graph reaches the transcript on every change without the agent electing to print it.

commands.acceptance: design.py acceptance --id R1 --altitude http|cli|browser|event|workflow|data --cmd '<check>' --red '<observed failure, before any code>'; later --green once it passes on its own; or --manual-owner '<who closes it>' --manual-evidence '<on what evidence>' for a requirement that genuinely cannot be automated
commands.node:
design.py node --slug --path

--purpose '' --role --verdict change|no_change|unsure [--stop-reason ABSORBED|MISPLACED|CROSSING|OPAQUE|VISITED|COMPLETE_UP|COMPLETE_DOWN|PASS_THROUGH|NO_ABSORPTION|CLEAR] [--belongs-in (required with MISPLACED)] [--depth N] [--evidence compiler|coverage|references|text|reasoning] [--why ...]
commands.behavior:
design.py behavior --slug --id B1 --statement '' --path

--symbol --status specified
commands.log: design.py log [--tail N]   # the decisions, and the reversals among them
commands.rebuild: design.py rebuild      # re-fold every log; use on resume
commands.show: design.py show [--level 0-4] [--full  (every traced node, no view budget)]

refusals: a verdict on a node with no purpose (principle 7)
a no_change verdict with no stop reason (principle 3)
a reversed verdict with no --why (principle 29c)
an acceptance record with neither --red nor --green - the requirement gate needs a check that was red before any code (principle 26)
a gate with no observed red evidence (principle 27)
an invariant on an application service (principle 19)
a task against a requirement that does not exist
closing a ticket with requirements still open (principle 11)
closing with a requirement marked done that has no recorded red evidence, or a behavior never gated (principle 2)
any decision on a closed ticket - appending would reopen it by side effect
any decision naming a task slug that does not exist - it would fold into nothing and look like it worked
a ticket ref or task slug that is not a dot-free, path-safe filename component
folding a decision log with an unreadable line - a dropped decision renders a stale conclusion
a MISPLACED stop with no --belongs-in - a behavior the purpose does not cover belongs in a node whose purpose does, or in one that does not exist yet (principle 7)
a repository recorded with no --aggregate - a repository stores exactly one aggregate root
a change or unsure verdict over a node that still carries a stop_reason, without --stop-reason CLEAR - the trace would keep showing a retracted stop
opening a task against a requirement with no recorded red acceptance evidence - no work on a requirement without a check that is red for it first (principle 26)
--stop-reason CLEAR with a no_change verdict - a no_change verdict requires a stop, so clearing one leaves the trace self-contradictory
a --manual-owner without --manual-evidence, or the reverse - half a manual-closure record is not a record
a --green whose --cmd differs from the command that went red - a different command is a different check and its red must be observed first
a --belongs-in that is neither a path nor 'new node: <path>' - a destination nothing can act on
manual-closure flags combined with --red or --green - two different decisions about how a requirement closes
--status green or gated on a behavior with no gate ledger entry - a status is a claim, the ledger entry with its observed red is the evidence
a task opened against a requirement that is done or descoped - that is not work this ticket is doing
--status green or gated on a behavior restated since it was gated - the gate proves the behavior as stated
descoping a requirement with no --why - descoping skips every evidence check, so the reason is the only record that it was a decision
closing with a requirement marked done that no behavior satisfies - a requirement with no behavior is not implemented (principle 8)
a behavior naming a requirement that does not exist - the requirement-to-behavior chain would be broken silently
re-recording an existing edge with a different kind - an edge carries one kind, and the second would be dropped silently or contradict the first
two nodes at one position in the ordered change set - it is the edit sequence, and a shared slot leaves it ambiguous which goes first
tooling.hook: hooks/hooks.json registers PostToolUse on Write|Edit|MultiEdit. Any write that lands in .design/ re-renders the tree and the index, so a direct edit by agent or human is caught too.
tooling.stop_reasons_note: design.py's --stop-reason choices are exactly phases[trace].stop_conditions, plus one value that is not a stop condition: CLEAR. CLEAR retracts a stop recorded by an earlier decision and is valid only when the verdict moves to change or unsure - a no_change verdict requires a real stop. Adding a stop condition to the trace phase means adding it to the CLI, or the normal stop becomes unrecordable and agents record a false ABSORBED; scripts/test_design.py asserts both halves of that mirror.
tooling.acceptance_note: Changing --cmd retracts any red_evidence and green transition recorded against the previous command: a different command is a different check, and evidence gathered against the old one proves nothing about the new one. Manual and automated closure are two modes of the same requirement and the latest decision picks one: recording a manual closure retracts any red/green evidence, and observing the check run retracts the manual closure. Neither is mixed, and a failure observed after a manual closure cannot be ignored by `close`. Changing altitude or harness retracts evidence exactly as changing --cmd does: each of the three redefines what is being checked.
tooling.gate_note: The behavior gate is enforced by the ledger, not by the status field. `close` requires a gate_ledger entry carrying observed red evidence for every behavior, and `behavior --status green|gated` refuses without one - so the gate cannot be passed by declaring that it was. A gate proves the behavior AS STATED: the ledger entry records the statement it gated, and restating a behavior afterwards invalidates its gate until a fresh red is observed.
